title: Swapping
summary: Moving an entire process out to disk to overcommit memory across more processes than physically fit, and why this whole-process approach is now mostly superseded by page-level swapping.

slides.markdown:
**Swapping**, in the classic sense, means moving an entire process's memory image out to disk to free up RAM for someone else, and copying it back later to resume. It's the original answer to a simple problem: what happens when more processes want to run than physically fit in memory at once?

Classic whole-process swapping is largely historical — modern virtual memory does the same overcommit trick at page granularity instead (demand paging). But the vocabulary and the underlying cost model carry straight over, and "swap" as a term survives today, confusingly, to mean something narrower: the disk-backed area pages get written to under memory pressure.

slides.sectionTitle: Swapping: moving an entire process between memory and disk
slides.markdown:
In classic swapping, a process that isn't currently runnable — blocked, waiting, or simply lower priority than something that needs the RAM right now — can be **swapped out**: its entire memory image is written to a reserved area of disk, and the physical frames it occupied become free for other processes.

When the process needs to run again, it's **swapped in**: the OS reads its full image back from disk into (possibly different) physical memory, and execution resumes as if nothing happened — because address binding is execution-time, the process's logical addresses don't need to know or care that the underlying physical location changed.

slides.sectionTitle: Why swapping exists: overcommitting memory across processes
slides.markdown:
Without swapping, the number of processes a system can run simultaneously is hard-capped by physical RAM — if ten processes need 1 GB each and the machine has 8 GB, the eleventh process simply cannot start. Swapping lifts that ceiling: the OS can keep more processes *in existence* than fit in RAM at once, by keeping only the ones that need to run right now resident, and parking the rest on disk.

This is the same overcommit idea that makes multiprogramming valuable in the first place — most processes spend a lot of their life waiting (on I/O, on a lock, on user input), so letting an idle process's memory sit on slow disk while a runnable one gets the RAM is a good trade, as long as swapping itself isn't happening too often.

slides.sectionTitle: Swap space vs regular file storage
slides.markdown:
The disk area used for swapping — a **swap partition** or a **swap file** — isn't a regular filesystem in the usual sense, even though a swap file physically lives inside one. It's treated as raw, OS-managed block storage: no directory structure, no filenames, just a large area the OS carves into slots for holding process memory images (or, in the modern page-level model, individual pages).

This matters for a subtle reason: swap space needs to be reserved and sized up front (or grown deliberately), because if the OS ever needs to swap something out and there's no swap space left, it has no fallback — which is exactly the scenario that leads to the OOM killer stepping in (covered in demand paging).

slides.sectionTitle: The cost of swapping — why it's slow
slides.markdown:
Moving an entire process's memory image is expensive in a way that's easy to underestimate. A process using 500 MB of RAM, swapped to a disk doing ~100 MB/s of sustained sequential I/O, takes roughly 5 seconds just to write out — and another 5 to read back in, before it can run a single instruction. Even on a fast NVMe SSD doing several GB/s, that's tens of milliseconds minimum, versus the tens-of-nanoseconds cost of a normal memory access — five to six orders of magnitude slower.

That gap is the entire reason systems try hard to avoid swapping at all: the moment swapping starts happening frequently rather than as a rare pressure-relief valve, whatever CPU time was saved by overcommitting memory is dwarfed by time spent waiting on disk.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: swapping vs paging-based demand paging
slides.markdown:
| | Classic whole-process swapping | Demand paging (modern virtual memory) |
|---|---|---|
| Unit moved | An entire process's memory image | Individual pages, only the ones actually touched |
| Cost per event | High — proportional to total process size | Low per page, but many small events instead of one big one |
| When it happens | Scheduling decision (this process isn't runnable right now) | On-demand, page by page, as memory pressure requires |
| What "swap" means today | Historical: moving whole processes | The disk-backed area individual evicted pages get written to |

Modern OSes still use the word "swap" constantly (swap usage, swappiness, swap partition) but almost never do classic whole-process swapping — see [Demand Paging](demand-paging) for how page-level eviction actually works day to day.

**Wrong belief:** "Swap usage is climbing, so the system must be thrashing."

**Why it's wrong:** non-zero, even substantial, swap usage can be completely healthy — it just means some genuinely cold, rarely-touched pages have been pushed to disk to make room for active ones, which is exactly what a well-tuned system should do. **Thrashing** is a much narrower, more severe condition: the system is spending more time paging pages in and out than doing useful computation, because the *active* working set no longer fits in RAM (full detail in [Thrashing & Working Set](thrashing-and-working-set)).

**Correct model:** watch page-in/page-out *rate*, not swap *usage*. High swap usage with a low, steady fault rate is fine; rapidly climbing swap I/O with CPU utilization dropping is the real thrashing signal.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading production swap metrics like a senior engineer
slides.markdown:
On a Linux box, `free -h` shows total swap used, and `vmstat 1` shows `si`/`so` (swap-in/swap-out rates per second) — the second is what actually tells you whether swapping is currently hurting you. A box that used 2 GB of swap an hour ago and hasn't touched it since is fine; a box with `si`/`so` climbing every second is actively paging live data back and forth, which is the expensive case.

A staff-level habit worth having: before treating "swap is being used" as an incident, check whether it's growing right now (active pressure) or just a static baseline (cold pages parked long ago). Cloud autoscaling and alerting rules that fire on raw swap-used percentage, rather than swap I/O rate, are a common source of noisy false-positive pages.
